newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers take aim at federal "corporate welfare".
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers take aim at federal "corporate welfare".

text.p: Charging that big business had been ripping off taxpayers far too long, a coalition of interest groups and key lawmakers Tuesday unveiled a 12-part hit list of "corporate welfare" programmes.

House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich, an Ohio Republican, is leading the unlikely coalition of liberal activists and conservative groups that wants to eliminate subsidies worth $11.5 billion over five years.

The biggest savings, $4 billion, would come from ending special highway construction projects that are pet projects of lawmakers. Another big ticket item, $3.5 billion in savings, would come from cutting back U.S. participation in an International Monetary Fund lending programme.
"This is another step to end welfare as we know it," Kasich said. "This is just, just the beginning of what we intend to do. No one should think that we are satisfied."

Other programmes on the hit list list include the Overseas Private Investment Corp. (OPIC), which provides loans and insurance to U.S. corporations that invest overseas. Barring new OPIC insurance or loans would save $281 million over five years.

The group wants to axe Forest Service road building to save more than $100 million; end aid to electric and telephone loans through the Agriculture Department Rural Utilities Service to save $190 million and end or modify the Animas La Plata public works project in Colorado to save $432 million.
Other targets are Energy Department programmes to reprocess plutonium and pay for oil, coal and gas research; Appalachian Regional Commission roads projects and clean coal technology.
Many of the programmes are familiar targets for budget cutters who have had them in their sights for ages. Kasich went after OPIC during the last session of Congress.
Lawmakers have also tried for years to end the Agriculture Department's Market Access Programme, another item on the list, which helps U.S. agribusiness promote products overseas.

What was unusual about the news conference was the picture of consumer advocate Ralph Nader and environmental activists standing shoulder-to-shoulder with Kasich and conservative groups such as the National Taxpayers Union.
"There will be a lot of sparks flying as a result of this effort ... but it's going to be a refreshing battle royale here on Capitol Hill," Nader said.

Also Tuesday, a bipartisan group of senators including Republican John McCain of Arizona and Democrat Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts announced they will introduce a bill setting up an independent commission to review corporate welfare.

Unlike the House, senators said they wanted to go after tax breaks for big corporations. Kennedy laid out a long list of business tax breaks that should be killed, complaining the federal government will lose $4.5 trillion due to tax subsidies over the next seven years.
"Surely if elderly couples depending on Medicare are required to pay additional premiums to balance the budget, wealthy corporations can be asked to contribute their fair share," Kennedy said.
Corporate welfare may be the mantra of both the left and right, but realistically, savings from such cuts are likely to be small in the context of any balanced budget.

Further, the groups are fighting entrenched interests, making the outlook for success questionable. Kasich's news conference was packed with lobbyists trying to figure out how his plans would affect their business.

Kasich predicted the new coalition would provide the needed impetus to make the overdue reforms. While calling the coalition historic and comparing it to David battling Goliath, he and his allies avoided taking on tax subsidies.
Kasich also said he wanted to eliminate federal sugar subsidy and ethanol aid but they did not make the top 12.
Liberal activists support cuts in corporate welfare to free up more money for domestic spending. Conservative activists see them as one more step toward a balanced budget.
